title: TA8-18531
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXXXXXXXXXXX (the claimant) is a citizen of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. She claims refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.1

The Chairperson's Gender Guidelines2 were taken into account when considering this case. All relevant factors, such as the social and cultural context in which the claimant found herself, along with the issues of state protection and changing country conditions were examined and guided with consideration of the Chairperson's Gender Guidelines.3 Furthermore, given the sensitive nature of the allegations the questions were asked in sensitive, respectful manner. A female Panel was provided for the hearing.

The claimant stated in her Personal Information Form (PIF)4 narrative that her father is violent and abusive and had made the family's lives miserable. She alleged that he tried to do many things to them, including burning down the house while they were still in it. The claimant provided an amendment5 to her PIF narrative. In that narrative, she stated that her father had abused her older half-sister, XXXXX. XXXXX eventually came to Canada in 2001 and the claimant's parents were divorced in 2002. After the divorce, the claimant's parents continued to live in the same home. The claimant alleged that after the divorce papers were served on her father, he grabbed her arm accusing her of being the cause of the divorce and hurt her. She and her mother went to the police station to file an assault charge and were told that they should come back if it happened again. The claimant alleges that in 2003, her father tried to choke her mother, who then hit him on the head with a mirror. They both went to the police and a statement was taken from her mother but the police did nothing. However, I note from the documents provided by counsel that a Protection Order6 was provided for her mother in 2003. The claimant alleged that her father tried to burn down the house on more than one occasion by leaving a pot burning on the stove. She alleged that he tried to flood the house well. She alleged that he has stated that one day he would kill them all and then kill himself. The claimant was fearful of taking a shower or bath because he would come inside the bathroom every time one of the family members was there. They slept with their bedroom door locked every night. They once found their father in their bedroom going through their stuff. The claimant recalls two times when her mother called the police on him and the police showed up at the house but he ran them off his property with a cutlass. The claimant alleged that her father would leave the music on very loud when they were sleeping, even though she suffered from migraines. She alleged that he walked around naked or scantily dressed to make them uncomfortable. She alleged that her father would peek in their bedroom. The claimant alleged that her father and the police officers at the XXXXXX police station were friends, therefore, the police didn't pay attention to their complaints. The claimant came to Canada on XXXXX, 2008 to visit her sister and remained.
I find that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. ANALYSIS Identity
The claimant's oral testimony and the supporting documentation filed,7 establish the claimant's identity as a national of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines.

The determinative issue in the claim is the availability of state protection and its adequacy and the state's willingness to effectively implement procedural and legislative frameworks in an effort to protect its citizens. In order for a refugee claim to be accepted by the Board, the Board must find a claimant has a well-founded fear of persecution in her country. The person must demonstrate not only that she has subjective fear, but that her fear has a valid or objective basis.8 The panel has found that the claimant's fear is not well-founded.

Several issues relating to this claim were considered. The determinative issues in the panel arriving at its negative decision were the availability of state protection and the issue of compelling reasons, which was raised by counsel. As well, the panel has considered that the claimant's problems and fears in Saint Vincent occurred when sharing a residence with her father. The panel has considered whether the claimant would suffer persecution or whether she is a person in need of protection in that her removal to Saint Lucia would subject her personally to a risk to her life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or whether there are substantial grounds to believe that her removal to Saint Lucia will subject her personally to a danger of torture, should she not reside with her father if she were to return to Saint Vincent.

The claimant stated that after her parents divorced, they continued to reside together. She was asked at the hearing whether her father ever physically or sexually assaulted her. She replied that he had only once hurt her in 2002, when he grabbed her arm at the time he received the divorce decree. The claimant was asked at the hearing why she, her mother and her sister XXXXXXX did not move out of the house to get away from the father. She replied that they did not have enough money to change residences. I note from the divorce petition prepared by the claimant's mother that it is stated that she could not reasonably be expected to live with the respondent9 and that the settlement of property and any other ancillary matters be heard in chambers. No evidence has been provided by the claimant regarding the distribution of property as ordered by the court. The claimant was asked why her mother was unable to leave the home. She replied that her mother could not afford to as she was not working after the divorce. The claimant was asked why she could not have moved away from the home after she completed school and began to work. She replied that she did not make enough money to pay for her own residence. The claimant was asked why she could not share a residence with other people or rent a room somewhere. She replied that this is not the way it is done in Saint Vincent. The claimant was asked about her sister, XXXXX XXX. She replied that before she left the country, XXXXXXX was attending college. The claimant was asked what the situation was for her mother and her sister now. She replied that they were both working. The claimant was asked why they still remained with the father, in the same house. She replied that they didn't have enough money to move. The claimant was asked whether she, her mother and her sister could all move to another residence, should the claimant return to Saint Vincent and all share the cost for that other residence. The claimant replied that they probably wouldn't have enough money to do that.

I have considered that the claimant continued to live with her father until she left the Saint Vincent in 2008. I have considered as well that her mother and her sister continue to live with the father to this day, eight years after the divorce even though the claimant states that they are both employed. I have also considered that the claimant has failed to provide anything documenting the settlement of property that was to be heard in chambers. I do not find it plausible that the claimant's mother would continue to remain in a life threatening situation with her two daughters for so many years after her divorce if indeed the lives of all three were truly at risk. I do not find it plausible that they would be unable to find another place to live within their own area if all three individuals were employed. As well, I do not find it plausible that the claimant would be unable to find a room to rent somewhere or a friend to stay with if she could not afford to rent a residence on her own. The claimant was asked whether she would have any fear of her father if she was not residing with him. The claimant replied that her father would still look for her and harass her. She stated that he had said that she could not go back to live in his house if she returned to Saint Vincent. She was asked whether he would come after her if she moved elsewhere in her area. She replied that she didn't know and that if she saw him on the street he would say something. She was asked whether her father would not bother her if her mother gave him the house. She replied 'maybe' but that her mother did not want to leave the house as she had nowhere to go.

I have considered that the claimant worked in Saint Vincent as a XXXXXXXXXXXX, that she has worked in Canada as a XXXXX and that she has been attending school in Canada, studying XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant would be able to work in Saint Vincent should she return to that country and that she would be able to find accommodation that she could afford notwithstanding that that accommodation would not be of the same standard as she had experienced before. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant would experience harassment from her father if she were not living with him, should she meet him on the street but that harassment would not amount to persecution or serious harm, taking into consideration that she had never been seriously harmed by her father in the past. Though she has stated that he tried to burn down the house by leaving pots cooking on the stove on two occasions and that he tried to flood the house on another occasion, I have nothing before me showing that these were actually serious attempts to kill any of the individuals in the home or to destroy the home. As noted before, the claimant, her mother and her sister continued to remain in the home with her father after these events occurred. I do not find it plausible that they would do so, if indeed these occurrences have been attempts on their lives.

The panel has considered the issue of state protection and finds that there is effective state protection in Saint Vincent and the claimant has failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence. In arriving at its decision, the panel considered the issue of whether the claimant's fear is objectively reasonable. To do so, the panel considered whether or not there is effective state protection in Saint Vincent, whether or not the claimant diligently or reasonably availed herself of that protection, or whether she has provided clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect.

In assessing the issue of state protection, the panel is guided by a number of cases from the Federal Court. The principles, enunciated hereafter, pertain to the case at hand and were accordingly applied. There is a presumption, except in situations where the state is in a complete breakdown, that it is capable of protecting its citizens. A claimant can rebut this presumption by providing clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect. The onus is on the claimant to approach the state for protection in situations where state protection might be reasonably forthcoming.10

No government is expected to guarantee perfect protection to all of its citizens at all times, and the fact that a state is not always successful in protecting its citizens, is not enough to justify a claim, especially where a state is making serious efforts to protect its citizens.11 Less than perfect protection is not a basis to determine that a state is either unwilling or unable to offer reasonable protection.12 Furthermore, the law states that the burden for the claimant to prove an absence of state protection is directly proportional to the level of democracy of that state.13 In a well-established democracy, such as Saint Vincent then, the claimant must do more than merely show that he or she went to see members of the police force and that those efforts were unsuccessful. The more democratic the state's institutions, the greater the onus on the claimant to show he or she has exhausted all courses of action available.14

The documentary evidence before the Board15 indicates that Saint Vincent is a democracy. There is an independent judiciary. The Board finds that Saint Vincent is in effective control of its territory and has in place a functioning security force to uphold the laws and constitution of the country. The Royal Saint Vincent police force is described as hierarchical, allowing for redress to a higher level if a complainant is dissatisfied with services. There is an oversight committee to monitor police activity and to hear public complaints about police misconduct.16

Saint Vincent has enacted legislation to address the problem of domestic violence through the Domestic Violence Proceedings Act (1994) and the Domestic Violence Summary Proceeding Act (1995).17 The latter act applies to all victims, regardless of marital status.18 The legislation enables the Court to issue Restraining Orders against aggressors and if the aggressor fails to respect the Restraining Order, the police can arrest him without a warrant.19 Victims are able to seek protective or restraining orders through the Family Court if a woman can show that her spouse or partner has committed, tried to commit or threatened to commit acts of physical, sexual or mental abuse.20 The Criminal Code has sanctions for rape or sexual assault, with significant sentences for convicted offenders.21 The Family Court also assists victims of domestic violence with locating temporary shelter.22 There are counsellors in the Family Court to assist with the preparation of documents for court proceedings, and to assist and counsel perpetrators and victims.

The police are now are more likely to view domestic violence as a criminal act rather than a private concern.23 The police force now has a significant number of female police officers and police officers in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines are trained to handle cases of domestic violence. An emphasis is placed on filing a report and initiating court proceedings if there is sufficient evidence.24 The coordinator of the Saint Vincent and the Grenadines Human Rights Association reports that police respond to all calls of domestic violence.25 The Saint Vincent and the Grenadines Human Rights Association holds national educational campaigns to make victims better aware of their legal rights and options.26 The President of the Family Court stated, "Offenders are arrested, charged and prosecuted by the police...."27 The statistics reflect the progress made. Protective orders are issued and the law is being applied, resulting in arrests, prosecutions and convictions of perpetrators.28 If gender-violence offenders go unpunished, it is reportedly often due to a culture where victims do not seek assistance from police or, when they do report, they do not follow through with the charges. This creates a cycle where police become reluctant to proceed criminally and instead encourage parties to settle.29 If a victim reports an offence to police, a written copy of the report is available to them.30 The Marion House is a social services agency that provides counselling, therapy and other services to victims of domestic violence.31

The population of Saint Vincent country is approximately 118,000 people and there are over 850 officers in the security forces.32 In his December 2004 budget address, Prime Minister and Minister of Finance Ralph Gonsalves noted that, among other things, the government had increased the number of officers within the police force, set up a serious crimes squad, rebuilt two police stations, declared that the government would be building two new police stations in 2005 and rebuilding or rehabilitating five more in the near future.33

With respect to violence against women, rape, including spousal rape, is illegal and the government enforced the law. Depending on the magnitude of the offense and the age of the victim, sentences for rape could be eight to ten years imprisonment. A possible sentence of life imprisonment was rarely used. During the year, police investigated 47 cases of rape, 8 cases of attempted rape and brought 18 cases to trial.34 The same report states that violence against women remained a serious problem. The Gender Affairs Division of the Ministry of National Mobilization, Social Development, NGO Relations, Family, Gender Affairs and Persons with Disabilities provided a referral and information service to domestic abuse victims, educating victims on the role of the police, legal affairs and Family Court in dealing with domestic violence as well as possible assistance from various NGOs. The Saint Vincent and the Grenadines Human Rights Association (SVGHRA) and other organizations conducted numerous seminars and workshops throughout the country to familiarize women with their rights. Development banks provided funding to the Caribbean Association for Feminist Research and Action for a program on domestic violence prevention, training and intervention. To counter the social pressures on victims to drop charges, some courts imposed fines against person who brought charges but did not testify.

While the documentary evidence indicates violence against women is a serious problem and that protection for victims is not perfect, it also describes this country as a functioning democracy, with a national police force, which includes 121 female police officers, improvement in the police response to violence against women and accessibility to legal remedies, which demonstrates that Saint Vincent is making serious efforts to address the problem of violence against women.

There is a report that the government operated an oversight committee to monitor police activity and to hear complaints about police misconduct. This committee reported to the Minister of National Security and to the Ministry of Legal Affairs and actively participated in investigations during the year.35 The Board must consider what this claimant did to avail herself of the protection of Saint Vincent and must also consider the response of the police.

The claimant stated that her mother made reports to the police but that nothing came out of those reports. The claimant has not provided any official corroborating documentation regarding any of these reports, stating that she and her mother were unable to get any of the documentation even though they tried. I note from the documentary evidence36 that a victim can obtain a copy of a complaint made to the police by applying to the Commissioner of police in writing care of the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. The claimant has provided a Protection Order issued for her mother37 stating that her father is prohibited from molesting her mother by using abusive language or behaving toward her in any other manner, which is of such nature and degree as to cause annoyance to her or result in ill-treatment of the applicant. This order was issued on XXXXXXXX, 2003. I find that this order is indicative that action had been taken on behalf of the claimant's mother by the authorities in Saint Vincent. The claimant has alleged that the police would do nothing regarding the complaints against her father because he had very strong connections within the government. She has alleged that he is a cousin of the XXXXXXXXXXXX, whose name is XXXXXXXXXXX and of the XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. She has provided no documentation to corroborate that these men hold these positions or that they are connected to her father. I find that this information would easily be available as these are high-level public positions and I take a negative inference from the claimant not providing corroborative documentation regarding the existence of these men and their positions within the government of Saint Vincent. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant's father is not connected to these men in high-level positions.

The claimant has stated that she never went to any other authority or organization in Saint Vincent regarding the many years of abuse that she suffered at the hands of her father and that is understandable considering her age at the time of the abuse. However, as she grew older, she never pursued any other avenue that could provide help. She never accessed the legal system for a protection order or approached any other organization or government authority.

A state cannot be considered to have failed to provide state protection when a claimant has failed to approach the state for protection. The adequacy of state protection cannot rest on the subjective fear of the claimant and a claimant cannot rebut the presumption of state protection in a functioning democracy by asserting only a subjective reluctance to engage the state.38 The onus is on the claimant to produce clear and convincing evidence that the police would not provide protection. In the absence of a compelling explanation, a failure to pursue state protection opportunities within the home state will usually be fatal to a refugee claim, at least where the state is a functioning democracy with the willingness and the apparatus necessary to provide a measure of protection to its citizens.39

I have considered the claimant's explanation that the police did nothing when her mother made a complaint because her father was well connected. However, I do note that I have earlier found, on a balance of probabilities, that her father did not have high-level connections and that the existence of a Protection Order for her mother showed that the government was attempting to provide protection to the claimant's mother.

Case law very clearly states that the expectation one can have from the state is adequate protection, not perfect protection. Perfect protection does not exist in any country and even in countries where state protection is excellent, perpetrators who want to seek revenge will do so. However, weighing what is before it, the preponderance of the objective, reliable and persuasive evidence regarding current country conditions suggest that, although not perfect, there is effective and adequate state protection in Saint Vincent, that Saint Vincent is making serious and genuine efforts to address the problem of domestic violence and that police are both willing and able to protect such victims. The Board is satisfied that were the claimant to return to Saint Vincent today and seek protection from authorities for violent acts perpetrated against her, protection would be reasonably forthcoming.

Counsel raised the issue of compelling reasons. Even though a claim for refugee protection may fail to meet the requirements of section 96 or section 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, where there has been a change in circumstances in the claimant's country of origin, such that the reasons for seeking protection have ceased to exist, subsection 108(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act permits the Board to review the case to determine if there are compelling reasons for allowing the claim. Jurisprudence of the Federal Court guides the Board in determining whether compelling reasons exist so as to trigger this section of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. The Board has a duty to consider the level of atrocity of the acts inflicted on the claimant, the repercussions on her physical and mental state, and to determine whether that experience alone constitutes a compelling reason not to return the claimant to her country of origin.40 In the case at hand, the Board is satisfied that there are no compelling reasons arising out of the claimant's history of the difficulties of her life with her father and that the claimant can return to her country of origin.

Persons who have been subjected to very serious persecution are seen to meet this criterion.41 The threshold necessary to determine "compelling reasons" is a high one.42 If the persecution was appalling, the experience alone is compelling reason enough not to return the claimant.43 Each case must be assessed and decided on its own merits, based on the totality of the evidence.44

The panel applied the principles enunciated in these decisions to the case at hand. The claimant was a minor at the time she was living with her father. Divorce, threats and harassment within a family for any woman, regardless of their age, would clearly have lasting effects, and certainly on a woman of a tender age, such as the claimant, it would have a greater effect. The panel accepts and acknowledges that living with her father negatively affected the claimant.

The panel has considered the fact that the claimant was able to function in Saint Vincent sufficiently enough to complete her education and to work. The panel has considered the information about the claimant here in Canada and has considered the psychological report45 of August 3, 2010. That report makes a finding of Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder. The report also states that the claimant is a hard-working and determined young woman who attempts to overcome many obstacles she has had to face.

The panel has also considered that in Canada the claimant has worked and is attending school. The panel acknowledges that the effects of abuse certainly have not terminated. However, with respect to this claimant, the panel cannot find that her mental state is such in that her ability to function has been significantly impaired. As well, the panel is satisfied if she required therapy, that it would be available to her in Saint Vincent.

The panel acknowledges the very negative effect that her upbringing has had on this claimant. It is logical and understandable that the claimant would fear harassment from her father because of her past experiences. However, the panel is satisfied, based on the documentary evidence noted earlier, that if threats were made by her father, the claimant would be able to go to the authorities and that assistance would be forthcoming.

In light of the foregoing, the panel is not persuaded that if the claimant's father or anyone else were to attempt to harm her, that there is clear and convincing evidence that the Government of Saint Vincent would not be reasonably forthcoming with adequate protection to protect the claimant if she were to return to Saint Vincent. While states are presumed to be capable of protecting their nationals, in this case Saint Vincent, it was open to the claimant, according to the law, to rebut the presumption with "clear and convincing evidence" as noted previously. The panel finds upon review of the evidence as a whole, including the testimony of the claimant, that she has not rebutted that presumption. Since finding that the claimant would be able to seek state protection, which based on documentary evidence is available to her, the claim must fail. As well, as noted earlier, the panel has found that compelling reasons do not exist for this claimant and, on a balance of probabilities, the claimant would be able to reside somewhere other than with her father in Saint Vincent and that at the most she would experience harassment from him, but that this would not amount to persecution.

Having considered all of the evidence and counsel's submissions, I find that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. Therefore, the Refugee Protection Division rejects her claim for refugee protection. "L. S. Hart" L. S.
